statement: Each correct answer on a test earns 5 points, wrong answers cost nothing, and every question has 5 choices. With no time left, a student must guess on 8 questions. On 3 of them she can rule out two choices; on the other 5 she can rule out none. On average, how many points do her 8 guesses earn?

choices.misconception: I thought ruling out two of the five choices left a fifty-fifty guess, so I used one half on those 3 questions.
I used a one-in-three chance on all 8 questions, as if she could rule out two choices on every one.
I treated ruling out two choices as making those 3 answers certain, so 15 points plus 5 from the other guesses.
I assumed every guess would be right, 8 x 5.

hints: Find the average points from one question of each kind.
Averages add across questions: for each question multiply the chance of being right by the points, then add. Ruling out choices changes the chance, not the points.
Three questions at a one-in-three chance and five questions at a one-in-five chance, each worth 5 points.

solutions.reliable: On a question with two choices ruled out, three remain, so a guess is right with probability 1/3 and earns 5 x 1/3 = 5/3 points on average. Three such questions give 5 points. On a question with nothing ruled out the chance is 1/5, worth 1 point on average, so five of them give 5 points. In total 5 + 5 = 10 points. The transferable idea: when wrong answers cost nothing, every guess has a positive average value, so never leave a blank, and ruling out choices raises that value.
solutions.elegant: Expected number of correct answers: 3 x 1/3 + 5 x 1/5 = 1 + 1 = 2, and 2 correct answers are worth 10 points.

whyOnTest: With no penalty for a wrong answer, a blank is worth nothing and a guess is worth more; this measures exactly how much more.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
